title: Statistics, populations and samples
summary: Where the word statistics comes from, descriptive vs inferential statistics, population vs sample, and when to use a sample or a census.

chunks.heading: Where 'statistics' comes from
chunks.explanation_md:
**Statistics** is derived from the Italian word **stato**, meaning *state*. A **statista** was a person involved with the affairs of the state, and statistics originally meant the **collection of facts** useful to the statista.

Today the word has moved beyond the state to **every state of human endeavor**: personal, business, social, environmental. It has also moved beyond collecting data towards **summarizing, displaying and analyzing data** into meaningful information that supports current and future decisions.
chunks.exam_line: Statistics comes from the Italian 'stato' (state); it now means summarizing, displaying and analyzing data into meaningful information for decisions.

chunks.heading: Descriptive vs inferential statistics
chunks.explanation_md:
Two statistical approaches:

- **Descriptive statistics** analyses and **summarises** data and organises it in some form, usually as **graphs and numerical summaries**. Example: **census**.
- **Inferential statistics** draws **conclusions about a population from a small sample**: methods of making decisions or predictions about a population based on a sample. Example: **exit poll**.

So a census describes everyone you counted; an exit poll asks a few voters and infers how everyone voted.

Methods of making decisions or predictions about a population based on a sample (e.g. exit poll).

chunks.heading: Population and sample
chunks.explanation_md:
Statistics is **the science of generalization from a part (the randomly chosen sample) to the whole (the population).**

- **Population:** the **entire group** you want to draw conclusions about.
- **Sample:** the **specific group** you will collect data from.

The slide's pairs:

| Population | Sample |
|---|---|
| Trend in advertisements for development jobs in India | The top 20 search results for such advertisements today |
| Songs from Bollywood movies | Songs from Bollywood movies that won the National Award |
| Participants of PGP in LMTSM | Participants with less than 1 years of experience |

The specific group that you will collect data from.

chunks.heading: When to use a sample and when a census
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide lists **conditions favouring a sample or a census**:

| Condition | Sample | Census |
|---|---|---|
| Budget | Small | Large |
| Time available | Short | Long |
| Population size | Large | Small |
| Variance in the characteristic | Small | Large |
| Cost of sampling errors | Low | High |
| Nature of measurement | Destructive | Non-destructive |
| Attention to individual cases | Yes | No |

Memory trick: a census needs **big money, long time and a small population**; a sample suits **tight budgets, short deadlines, huge populations and destructive testing** (you cannot test-destroy every unit).
chunks.exam_line: A sample is favoured by a small budget, short time, large population, small variance, low cost of sampling errors and destructive measurement; a census by the opposite.

questions.stem: Trace how the meaning of the word 'statistics' has changed, from its origin to today.
questions.model_answer_md:
The word started with governments and now covers almost everything.

- **Origin:** from the Italian word **stato**, meaning **state**. A **statista** was a person involved with the affairs of the state.
- **Original meaning:** the **collection of facts** useful to the statista.
- **Today (wider scope):** it covers **every state of human endeavor**: personal, business, social, environmental.
- **Today (wider work):** it has moved beyond data collection to **summarizing, displaying and analyzing data** into meaningful information for **current and future decisions**.

So statistics grew from counting facts for the state to a decision tool for everyone.

questions.stem: Discuss the conditions that favour the use of a sample over a census, and vice versa, as given on the 'Sample Versus Census' slide.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **census** studies the whole population; a **sample** studies a specific group drawn from it. The slide lists seven conditions that tip the choice.

| Condition | Favours a sample | Favours a census |
|---|---|---|
| **Budget** | Small | Large |
| **Time available** | Short | Long |
| **Population size** | Large | Small |
| **Variance in the characteristic** | Small | Large |
| **Cost of sampling errors** | Low | High |
| **Nature of measurement** | Destructive | Non-destructive |
| **Attention to individual cases** | Yes | No |

**Reading the table:**
- **Resources:** a **small budget** and **short time** push towards a sample; a census needs **big money and a long time**.
- **Population:** a **large population** is impractical to count fully, so sample; a **small population** can be covered completely.
- **Variance:** if the characteristic **varies little**, a sample already captures it; **large variance** needs the whole population.
- **Risk of error:** if a **sampling error would be costly**, a census is safer.
- **Destructive measurement:** if testing destroys the item, you **cannot test every unit**, so a sample is the only option.
- **Individual cases:** when attention to individual cases is needed, the slide marks sample as favoured.

**Conclusion:** a census suits big budgets, long timelines, small and varied populations and costly errors; a sample suits tight budgets, short deadlines, huge populations and destructive testing.

rubric.point: Budget: small favours sample, large favours census
Time: short favours sample, long favours census
Population size: large favours sample, small favours census
Variance: small favours sample, large favours census
Cost of sampling errors: low sample, high census
Destructive measurement favours sample; attention to individual cases

questions.stem: Florida had more than 18 million residents, yet the Department of Tourism surveyed a sample of 868. Using the sample versus census conditions and the ideas of population, sample and inferential statistics, explain why this design makes sense.
questions.model_answer_md:
The Florida survey is a clear case of studying a **part** to learn about the **whole**.

**Population and sample:**
- **Population:** the entire group we want conclusions about: qualified adult residents of Florida, a state of more than 18 million people.
- **Sample:** the specific group data is collected from: **868** respondents reached by telephone.

**Why a sample, not a census:**
- **Population size: large.** More than 18 million residents favours a sample.
- **Budget and time:** contacting every household would need a **large budget** and a **long time**; a telephone sample fits a **small budget** and **short time**.
- **Cost of sampling errors:** a sample is the sensible choice when the cost of a sampling error is **low**; a census is kept for cases where that cost is high.

**Making the sample trustworthy:**
- The households were **stratified** by north, central and south Florida, so all regions are included.
- **Computerized random digit dialing** and the **next birthday method** keep selection random, giving a **representative sample**.

**What kind of statistics:** this is **inferential statistics**: drawing **conclusions about a population from a small sample**, like the slide's **exit poll** example. A census would be descriptive statistics, summarising everyone.

**Conclusion:** statistics is the science of generalization from a randomly chosen sample to the population, and the Florida design (large population, limited resources, random stratified sample of 868) is exactly that idea in practice.

rubric.point: Population: Florida residents (18 million plus); sample: 868
Large population favours a sample
Small budget and short time favour a sample; census only when sampling error is costly
Stratified, random digit dialing, next birthday: representative
Inferential statistics: conclusions about a population from a sample, like an exit poll
Generalization from part to whole
